answer: In this 1989 NLSY79 young-adult sample (N=12,686, ages 24–32), older age is associated with a lower likelihood of dissaving — withdrawing more from savings than putting in. Each additional year of age is associated with about 4% lower odds of dissaving (OR ≈ 0.96 per year, 95% CI 0.94–0.98, p<0.001), corresponding to roughly a 0.8 percentage-point lower probability per year (average marginal effect ≈ −0.008, SE 0.0016). The age profile is weakly non-linear (LR test for the quadratic p≈0.03 unadjusted / 0.05 adjusted): the predicted probability of dissaving rises slightly through the mid-20s (peak ≈ age 25–26) and then declines roughly monotonically from ≈0.26 at ages 24–26 to ≈0.19 by age 32 (adjusted quadratic predictions: 0.257@24, 0.260@25, 0.248@28, 0.225@30, 0.193@32; bootstrap 95% CIs 0.23–0.28@24, 0.23–0.26@28, 0.16–0.21@32). The gradient is essentially unchanged after controlling for INCOME, GENDER, BLACK, HISPANIC and BMI (unadjusted OR 0.959 vs adjusted OR 0.959), so it is not a compositional artifact of observed covariates, and it is robust to probit, age-banding (24–27/28–30/31–32: 0.237/0.209/0.195) and BMI-winsorization. Caveat: the negative gradient is concentrated in the ≈31% of observations whose INCOME equals the sample mean (consistent with mean-imputation; that subgroup dissaves far less, 0.112 vs 0.292, and its share rises with age); within the remaining 69% of rows the age gradient is flat-to-weakly-positive and non-significant, and controlling for the imputed-flag or dropping the cluster makes the age terms non-significant. The association is therefore suggestive and fragile to INCOME data quality, and strictly correlational (cohort/age effects inseparable). Consistent with — but not proof of — rising future-orientation/patience with age, a plausible interpretive framing given cross-sectional self-reported data.

payload.hypothesis: Older age in this 1989 NLSY79 young-adult sample is associated with a lower likelihood of dissaving: odds ~4% lower per year of age (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.94-0.98), with a weakly non-linear profile — predicted probability peaks near age 25-26 then declines roughly monotonically from ~0.26 (ages 24-26) to ~0.19 (age 32). The gradient is unchanged after adjusting for income, gender, race and BMI and holds under probit, age-banding and BMI-winsorization, but is concentrated in the ~31% of rows with mean-imputed income and is non-significant within the non-imputed subsample, so it is a fragile, strictly correlational association.
payload.workflow: Binary logistic regression of DISSAVED on age (linear and centered-quadratic AGE_C+AGE_C2), unadjusted and adjusted for INCOME, GENDER, BLACK, HISPANIC, BMI; linear-vs-quadratic adjudicated by nested LR test and AIC/BIC; age effect reported as OR/year (linear) and as AMEs and predicted P(DISSAVED) at ages 24/28/32 with delta-method and 100-replicate bootstrap CIs; robustness: probit, age banding (24-27/28-30/31-32), BMI winsorization at 99th pct, INCOME imputation-cluster sensitivity (flag and drop), and an optional 3-category multinomial.
